items.summary: BEIR comprises 18 publicly available zero-shot evaluation datasets spanning 9 heterogeneous retrieval tasks, plus MS MARCO reported separately as the in-domain training reference.

Dataset/task selection was guided by four factors: diverse tasks (query/document length variation), diverse domains (generic to specialized), sufficient task difficulty, and diverse annotation strategies (crowd, expert, community feedback).
Across BEIR, corpus sizes range 3.6k-15M documents, average query length ranges 3-192 words, and average document length ranges 11-635 words.
BEIR introduces a standardized data format (corpus, queries, qrels) and converts every included dataset into it.
items.value: corpus/queries/qrels standard format

items.summary: nDCG@10 was chosen as the single comparable metric across all tasks (binary and graded relevance), computed with the Python interface of the official TREC evaluation tool (pytrec_eval).
items.value: nDCG@10, computed with pytrec_eval

items.summary: Only 8 of the 19 datasets (including MS MARCO) provide training data, illustrating the practical importance of zero-shot retrieval benchmarking.
items.value: 8/19 datasets have training data

items.summary: All BEIR datasets except ArguAna have short queries (a single sentence or 2-3 keywords).
items.value: all except ArguAna have short queries

items.summary: Pairwise weighted-Jaccard word-overlap between BEIR datasets is generally low, indicating BEIR datasets span diverse, largely non-overlapping vocabularies/domains.
items.value: generally low overlap across domains

items.summary: Illustrative weighted-Jaccard overlap values from Figure 2's heatmap: two Wikipedia-derived datasets (DBPedia, HotpotQA) overlap much more (~0.89) than a Wikipedia dataset and a biomedical dataset (DBPedia, NFCorpus, ~0.13).
items.conditions: read from Figure 2 heatmap text row 'DBPedia 0.16 0.15 0.13 0.44 0.89 ...' in column order TREC-COVID,BioASQ,NFCorpus,NQ,HotpotQA,...
items.notes: Figure 2 is a heatmap; these values were read from its text dump, not from machine-readable data, hence strength=soft despite being printed numbers.

items.summary: Due to transformer length limits, only the first 512 word pieces of each document were used across all neural architectures in every experiment.
items.value: 512 word pieces max, all neural models

items.summary: BM25 baseline configuration: Anserini implementation, default Lucene parameters k=0.9, b=0.4; title (if available) and passage indexed as separate fields.

items.notes: Verbatim numbers as extracted; column alignment reconstructed and cross-validated (see summary) because the raw text extraction interleaves the original table's columns. SCIDOCS corpus is given here as 25,657 while Appendix D.8 prose describes it approximately as 'a corpus of 30K held-out pool of scientific papers' (line 876) -- treated as a rounded description, not a numeric conflict.

items.summary: Zero-shot average performance vs. BM25 (nDCG@10, % relative change, last row of Table 2) for the 9 non-BM25 systems.
items.conditions: average across the 18 BEIR zero-shot test datasets, nDCG@10

items.summary: In-domain MS MARCO nDCG@10 scores (Table 2 first column; ‡ marks in-domain training).
BM25 underperforms neural approaches on the in-domain MS MARCO evaluation by 7-18 points, yet the paper reports it as a strong zero-shot generalization baseline on BEIR.
items.value: BM25 underperforms by 7-18 points in-domain on MS MARCO

items.summary: No single retrieval approach consistently outperforms all other approaches on all BEIR datasets.
items.value: no single approach dominates

items.summary: The in-domain performance of a model does not correlate well with its zero-shot generalization capability; models fine-tuned with identical training data can generalize differently.
items.value: in-domain accuracy does not predict OOD generalization

items.summary: DeepCT and SPARTA both perform well in-domain on MS MARCO but 'completely fail to generalize', underperforming BM25 on nearly all BEIR datasets.
items.value: DeepCT/SPARTA fail to generalize despite strong in-domain performance

items.summary: docT5query (document expansion) outperforms BM25 on 11 of 18 BEIR datasets while remaining competitive on the rest.
items.value: docT5query beats BM25 on 11/18 datasets

items.summary: Dense retrievers (esp. ANCE, TAS-B) perform strongly on some datasets but significantly worse than BM25 on many others; dense retrievers underperform particularly under large domain shift (e.g. BioASQ) or task shift (e.g. Touché-2020).
items.value: dense retrievers underperform under large domain/task shift

items.summary: DPR, the only evaluated model not trained on MS MARCO, has the worst overall generalization on the benchmark.
items.value: DPR worst overall generalization

items.summary: BM25+CE (cross-attentional re-ranking) outperforms BM25 on almost all datasets (16/18), failing only on ArguAna and Touché-2020, two tasks very different from the MS MARCO training data.
items.value: BM25+CE beats BM25 on 16/18; fails only on ArguAna and Touché-2020

items.summary: ColBERT (late interaction) performs a bit weaker than BM25+CE but still outperforms BM25 on 9 of 18 datasets.
items.value: ColBERT beats BM25 on 9/18 datasets

items.summary: Cross-attention and cross-attention-like operations (re-ranking, late interaction) appear important for good out-of-distribution generalization.
items.value: cross-attention(-like) interaction associated with better OOD generalization

items.summary: TAS-B provides the best zero-shot generalization among dense retrievers: it outperforms ANCE on 14/18 datasets and DPR on 17/18 datasets.
items.value: TAS-B beats ANCE 14/18, DPR 17/18

items.summary: The paper speculates TAS-B's stronger generalization stems from its training setup: in-batch negatives combined with a Margin-MSE loss under a strong-teacher-ensemble knowledge-distillation setup.
items.value: TAS-B generalization attributed (speculatively) to training loss/setup
items.notes: Authors use 'we speculate' -- explicitly hedged in the source.

items.summary: TAS-B underperforms ANCE by 17.3 points on TREC-COVID and by 7.8 points on Touché-2020.

Underlying nDCG@10 values behind the TAS-B/ANCE gap (Table 2): TREC-COVID TAS-B=0.481, ANCE=0.654 (diff 0.173); Touché-2020 TAS-B=0.162, ANCE=0.240 (diff 0.078). These exactly reproduce the 17.3-point and 7.8-point gaps stated in prose (E026), cross-validating the table reconstruction.
TAS-B and ANCE retrieve top-10 documents of very different median length: on TREC-COVID, TAS-B's median is ~10 words vs. ANCE's ~160 words; on Touché-2020, ~14 vs. ~89 words.

Controlled ablation (Appendix H): two otherwise-identical distilbert-base-uncased models trained on MS MARCO, differing only in similarity function (cosine vs. dot product). The dot-product model achieves the largest gain on TREC-COVID, +15.3 points nDCG@10; on most other datasets it performs worse than the cosine-similarity model.
items.value: TREC-COVID: +15.3-point gain for dot-product vs. cosine-similarity model
items.conditions: identical training setup, only similarity function changed

items.summary: Table 10 nDCG@10 values underlying the cosine-vs-dot-product ablation: TREC-COVID cosine=0.482, dot=0.635 (diff 0.153, matches the stated 15.3-point gain exactly); Signal-1M(RT) cosine=0.261, dot=0.243; FEVER cosine=0.670, dot=0.685.

Cosine-similarity models systematically prefer retrieving shorter documents than dot-product models across BEIR datasets, most severely on TREC-COVID, where ~42k of ~171k papers consist only of a title with no abstract and are disproportionately retrieved by the cosine-similarity model.
items.value: cosine-similarity models prefer shorter documents; dot-product models prefer longer ones

items.summary: Relevance judgement scores are not uniformly distributed over document length across BEIR datasets: some datasets annotate longer documents as more relevant, others annotate shorter documents as more relevant.
items.value: relevance vs. document length pattern varies by dataset

items.summary: GenQ (synthetic-query domain adaptation on top of TAS-B) outperforms TAS-B on specialized domains (scientific publications, finance, StackExchange) but performs weaker than TAS-B on broader/generic domains such as Wikipedia.
items.value: GenQ helps specialized domains, hurts broad/generic domains relative to TAS-B

items.summary: Efficiency measurement setup: 1 million documents randomly sampled from DBPedia; exact search for dense models; ColBERT uses approximate nearest neighbor search (as in its original setup); CPU = 8-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8168 @ 2.70GHz; GPU = single Nvidia Tesla V100, CUDA 11.0.

The best out-of-distribution generalizers (re-ranking top-100 BM25 hits; late-interaction) are also the slowest at inference (>350ms). Dense retrievers are 20-30x faster (<20ms). On CPU, sparse models are fastest (20-25ms).

Lexical, re-ranking and dense methods have the smallest index sizes (<3GB for 1M DBPedia documents). SPARTA (30k-dim sparse vectors) needs the second-largest index; ColBERT (multiple 128-dim vectors per document) needs the largest.
items.value: index size ranking: SPARTA 2nd-largest, ColBERT largest, others <3GB

items.summary: At larger scale, ColBERT would require ~900GB to index the ~15M-document BioASQ corpus, versus 18GB for BM25.

Many BEIR datasets show a lexical bias in how their relevance judgements were pooled: e.g. BioASQ candidates were retrieved for annotation via lexical term-matching with boosting tags; Signal-1M(RT) used 7 of 8 lexical-term-matching techniques to retrieve tweets for annotation.
items.value: BioASQ and Signal-1M annotation pools built with lexical retrieval

items.summary: Hole@10 (share of a system's top-10 hits never seen by annotators) on TREC-COVID, by system: BM25 6.4%, DeepCT 19.4%, SPARTA 12.4%, docT5query 2.8%, DPR 30.6%, ANCE 14.4%, TAS-B 31.8%, ColBERT 12.4%, BM25+CE 1.6%.
TREC-COVID nDCG@10 before ('original, w/ holes') and after manual re-annotation ('annotated, w/o holes') of the 980 previously-unjudged pairs, by system.
items.conditions: TREC-COVID, Table 4, 980 manually annotated query-document pairs added

items.summary: After re-annotation, lexical systems changed only slightly (e.g. docT5query 0.713→0.714), while non-lexical systems improved substantially (ANCE 0.654→0.735, i.e. 6.7 points above BM25's annotated score; ColBERT improved 5.8 points).
items.value: lexical systems ~unchanged; non-lexical systems improve substantially after de-biasing annotation

items.summary: 980 query-document pairs were manually annotated by the paper's authors, following the original TREC-COVID annotation guidelines, blind to which system had retrieved each pair (to avoid preference bias).
items.value: 980 pairs manually annotated, blind to source system

items.summary: Even though many diverse systems contributed to the TREC-COVID annotation pool, the pool remained biased toward lexical approaches.
items.value: TREC-COVID pool still lexically biased despite diverse contributing systems

items.summary: Appendix B limitations, quoted/paraphrased: (1) all 18 datasets are English-only, citing multilingual work as future direction; (2) documents are limited to roughly a few hundred words (transformer 512-wordpiece limit), so long-document retrieval is untested; (3) only pure textual signals are used, not auxiliary ranking signals (PageRank, recency, authority, click-through); (4) evaluation covers only one or two document fields, not full multi-field retrieval; (5) the benchmark targets models that generalize broadly, so a task-specific specialized model could still outperform generalist models on an individual task.

Reproducibility checklist admissions: (3c) no error bars/seed-variance reported, because most evaluated systems are third-party pre-trained checkpoints without accessible training code, making re-training infeasible in many cases; (3d) GPU/CPU hardware types are reported but total compute used is not.

Checklist admission: the authors did not check whether the underlying (re-used, mostly public) datasets contain personally identifiable or offensive content, citing the difficulty of checking more than 50 million documents and the risk of altering the datasets.
items.value: no PII/offensive-content screening performed (checklist 4e)

items.summary: Related-work characterization of MultiReQA: 8 QA datasets evaluating sentence-level answer retrieval given a question; only one task type; 5 of 8 datasets are Wikipedia-based; 6 of 8 have fewer than 100k candidate sentences, a scale the paper says favors dense over lexical retrieval per a cited prior finding.
items.value: MultiReQA: 8 QA datasets, single task, mostly Wikipedia, mostly <100k candidates

items.summary: Related-work characterization of KILT: 5 knowledge-intensive tasks comprising 11 datasets in total; retrieval is involved but is not the primary task; documents are retrieved only from Wikipedia.
items.value: KILT: 5 tasks/11 datasets, retrieval not primary, Wikipedia-only

items.summary: The paper states, hedged as 'to our knowledge', that BEIR is the first broad, zero-shot information retrieval benchmark.
items.value: 'To our knowledge, BEIR is the first broad, zero-shot information retrieval benchmark.'

items.summary: Model/architecture families and the ten representative systems evaluated: (i) Lexical: BM25. (ii) Sparse: DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query. (iii) Dense: DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ. (iv) Late-interaction: ColBERT. (v) Re-ranking: BM25+CE (MiniLM cross-encoder).
docT5query: T5(base) model trained on MS MARCO generates synthetic queries appended to each document (40 queries/document), then retrieved with BM25 (default Anserini parameters).
items.value: T5-base doc-expansion, 40 synthetic queries/doc, then BM25

items.summary: DPR: bi-encoder trained with one BM25 hard negative plus in-batch negatives; the 'Multi' variant used (bert-base-uncased trained on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions and CuratedTREC, including titles) outperformed the single-NQ variant in this setting.
items.value: DPR-Multi, bert-base-uncased, 4 QA datasets, BM25 hard negative + in-batch negatives

items.summary: ANCE: RoBERTa bi-encoder trained on MS MARCO for 600K steps, using hard negatives mined from an approximate nearest neighbor index of the corpus that updates during fine-tuning.
items.value: RoBERTa bi-encoder, ANN hard negatives, MS MARCO 600K steps

items.summary: TAS-B: bi-encoder trained with Balanced Topic-Aware Sampling under dual supervision from a cross-encoder and a ColBERT model, combining a pairwise Margin-MSE loss with an in-batch negative loss.
items.value: bi-encoder, Balanced Topic Aware Sampling, cross-encoder+ColBERT dual supervision, Margin-MSE + in-batch negative loss

items.summary: GenQ: unsupervised domain-adaptation approach. A T5(base) model is fine-tuned on MS MARCO for 2 epochs, then generates 5 synthetic queries per target-domain document (top-k=25, top-p=0.95 sampling), capped at 100K target documents per dataset; the TAS-B model is then further fine-tuned with in-batch negatives on the synthetic query/document pairs. A separate model is trained per target task.
items.value: T5-base query generator -> synthetic query/doc pairs -> continued TAS-B fine-tuning, per-task model

items.summary: ColBERT: encodes queries/documents into bags of contextualized token embeddings; late interaction aggregated via sum-of-max-similarity. Used end-to-end: faiss ANN retrieves top candidates (faiss depth=100), then ColBERT re-ranks via the late-interaction score. Trained as bert-base-uncased, max sequence length 300, on MS MARCO for 300K steps.
items.value: bert-base-uncased, seq len 300, MS MARCO 300K steps, faiss ANN depth 100 + MaxSim re-rank

items.summary: BM25+CE: re-ranks the top-100 hits from first-stage Anserini BM25 using a 6-layer, 384-hidden MiniLM cross-encoder (chosen as the best of 14 publicly available cross-attentional re-rankers tested on MS MARCO), trained via knowledge distillation from an ensemble of BERT-base, BERT-large and ALBERT-large teacher models.
items.value: MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder reranks BM25 top-100, best of 14 tested, distilled from BERT-base/BERT-large/ALBERT-large ensemble

items.summary: DeepCT: bert-base-uncased trained on MS MARCO learns term weights, producing a pseudo-document of keywords weighted by learned term frequency, then retrieved with BM25 (default Anserini parameters, found to work better than tuned MS MARCO parameters in this setting).
items.value: bert-base-uncased term-weight learner -> pseudo-document -> BM25 (default Anserini params)

items.summary: SPARTA: computes similarity between non-contextualized query-token embeddings and contextualized document-token embeddings from BERT, pre-computable into a 30,000-dimensional sparse vector per document (2,000 non-zero entries used); re-implemented by the authors (fine-tuning DistilBERT on MS MARCO) because the original implementation was not publicly available.
items.value: re-implemented (original unavailable); DistilBERT fine-tuned on MS MARCO; 30k-dim sparse vector, 2000 non-zero entries

items.summary: Argument retrieval task definition: ranking argumentative texts by relevance to a topical query; ArguAna retrieves the best counterargument to a given argument (arguments/counterarguments scraped from an online debate portal); Touché-2020 is a conversational argument-retrieval task over the args.me corpus.
items.value: ArguAna = best-counterargument retrieval; Touché-2020 = conversational argument retrieval over args.me

items.summary: Citation-prediction task definition (SCIDOCS): given a paper title as query, retrieve papers it cites; SCIDOCS uses the 'direct-citations' task (one of seven tasks in the original SCIDOCS paper) as the best fit for retrieval evaluation, with 1,000 query papers each paired with 5 relevant (cited) and 25 randomly sampled non-cited papers.
items.value: SCIDOCS direct-citations: 1000 query papers, 5 relevant + 25 random negatives each

items.summary: DPR's Multi-model training data includes NQ, one of the 18 nominally 'zero-shot' BEIR datasets; its NQ score in Table 2 is marked with ‡ (in-domain), unlike DPR's scores on the other 17 zero-shot datasets.
items.value: DPR's NQ evaluation is partially in-domain (‡ marked in Table 2), unlike its other zero-shot scores
